pr.title: Plan showing projects proposed in open pull requests
pr.head: d132e37bc76cc4f44ee9143a5dc7cbb8ea3bfe92

summary: Projector's site has a Projects page that lists every plan under docs/projects/ on the default branch. Projector writes each new plan as a pull request so people review it before it merges, so while a plan is in review the Projects page, the site's search, and the links from review pages all leave it out. The plan's text is already on the site, though: each published summary stores its pull request's diff as diff.patch, and the diff of a new file holds every line of that file.
This pull request adds one plan, proposed-projects, at status: ready and priority: next. It changes no code. The plan has the site build do the following:

1. Find proposed plans. For each open pull request whose branch is in this repository, not a fork, the build reads its newest summary and picks each readme.md that the diff adds as a new file under the projects directory.
  2. Rebuild and parse them. It rebuilds the file's text from the diff's added lines and parses it with the same code that project list runs, so a proposed plan loads exactly when the same plan would load once merged.
  3. Show them as proposed. It lists each one on the Projects page in its status group with a Proposed badge, and opens its page at projects/<name>/ with a banner that names the pull request.
  4. Deploy when a pull request closes. The generated site workflow gains a pull_request_target trigger on closed, so the site drops a proposed plan as soon as its pull request merges or closes. project check warns while a repository still has the older generated workflow.

The build reads only the summaries plus one more field in the status query it already makes, so it makes no new GitHub request. A plan already on the default branch always wins over a proposal, and the lowest pull request number wins a name that two pull requests propose.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Summary: the review page data that project summary publish stores on refs/projector/summaries, with the pull request's diff beside it.
  • Checkout: the branch the site is built from, the default branch on a deploy.
  • Proposed project: a plan that the newest summary of an open, non-fork pull request adds and the checkout lacks.
  • Nested project: a project inside another project's folder, such as alpha/beta.
  • pull_request_target: a GitHub Actions event that runs the workflow from the default branch, with that branch checked out, rather than from the pull request's code.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
• 15cb40d, changes requested. One finding: a step dropped a proposed nested plan whose top-level folder has no plan, though the checkout lists such a plan. One suggestion: skip hidden folders.
  • d132e37, clean. Both are fixed. This head also excludes forks and adds the deploy on close. One suggestion remains: test the project check warning against every earlier workflow shape.

groups.title: The proposed-projects plan
groups.kicker: A ready plan for listing plans that open pull requests add
intro: The plan is the whole change. Read it in order: § 1 says what the site misses today, § 2 gives the design step by step, with the workflow change in § 2.4, § 3 gives the reasons and the rejected options, and § 4 lists the tests the implementing pull request must add.

Because the plan is at ready, it claims that someone can implement it without asking further questions. Check each claim it makes about the current code and about GitHub, since an implementer will build on them.

files.note: The new plan. It names the functions it changes in src/projector/site/__init__.py, src/projector/summary.py, src/projector/core.py, src/projector/cli.py, and site/src/site.ts, and the site workflow.

checks.text: § 2.1 is the build's algorithm. Today build_summaries links each summary to projects while it reads the summaries, and asks GitHub for each pull request's state afterwards. The plan reorders that: read, ask for states, find proposed plans, then link over both lists.

Step 2 only moves an existing call and adds a field to it. I read build_summaries: it calls status_lookup once for each pull request, after linking, and the statuses test asserts one call per pull request. PR_STATUS_QUERY already returns state, base, and reviews, so isCrossRepository rides on the same query.

The nested-plan rule now matches the checkout. I built a site from a checkout with omega/x/readme.md and no omega/readme.md: site_projects warns about omega and still lists omega/x, which is what this step and the § 4 row now expect.
Step 9 leaves out Markdown under a folder whose name starts with ., as pages_under does for a checkout project.
§ 2.3 keeps the word in one constant, PROPOSED, and adds a badge proposed link to the pull request's review page wherever the site lists the project.

§ 2.4 is the workflow change. Today the site deploys on a summary publish, a push to the default branch that changes watched paths, or a manual run, so a closed pull request stays on the site until something else deploys.

I walked the concurrency expression for each event. repository_dispatch, push, workflow_dispatch, and a same-repository close all get pages. A fork's close, including one whose fork was deleted so head.repo is null, gets fork-<run id>, and the job's if on the next line skips it.

GitHub's 2025-11-07 changelog says that from 2025-12-08 a pull_request_target run takes its workflow file, GITHUB_REF, GITHUB_SHA, and checkout from the default branch, and checks environment rules against it. The site action's actions/checkout@v4 takes no ref, and this repository's github-pages environment allows only main, so a close deploys from main, even for a stacked pull request.
The site-workflow-outdated warning is for every earlier generated shape. The § 4 row on line 523 tests only today's shape; the review suggests adding the shapes in PREVIOUS_WORKFLOWS.

Proposed content is served as Markdown only. showHtml loads an HTML page in an iframe on the site's own origin without a sandbox attribute, so an unmerged page's script could read the rest of the site.

I read parse_diff in src/projector/summary.py: it sets new from new file mode, keeps every added line, and records \ No newline at end of file as a meta line, so new_file_text can rebuild a new file from its output.
